t: The first phone screen explains how the site is built, not what it is about
x: A contact who taps a link cannot tell in one screen that this is a publication about AI agents, security and publishing, or why they were sent it.

t: The home page is 59 phone screens long, with 845 links
x: The front page tries to show everything, so it chooses nothing for the reader. Nobody scrolls 59 screens; the curation is invisible.

t: All three rating scales start on 3
x: Neither the reader nor the author can tell "not rated" from "useful". Every rating collected so far is ambiguous.

t: Ratings never reach the author
x: The first contacts sent to the site teach the author nothing about what landed.

t: Opening an article charges a penny with no notice
x: The first thing a new reader learns about the reading meter is that their balance dropped without being told.

t: Nothing shows real money moving
x: Readers and publishers asking "is this a real business?" find no answer.

t: It is unclear how a writer gets paid
x: Writers and publishers, the people the meter is pitched to, cannot see where their share comes from.

t: No contact for a pilot on the Replicate page
x: The one reader ready to act has nowhere to go. A blocking finding of the synthetic-user study.

t: Two domains claim to be canonical for the same article
x: Search engines split the article's standing between two copies, and readers can land on either.

t: The founder page says "the picks above" and no picks render on a phone
x: The page a founder is sent to points at content that is not there, on the first visit, which is the only one that matters.

t: Setting location.hash inside a vault app re-navigates the frame: every link silently dead
x: An app that works when opened as a file ships to readers with no working navigation, and nothing errors.

t: Scrolling back up a little puts focus in the address bar and opens the keyboard
x: The reader was not asking to go anywhere, and loses half the screen to a keyboard. Worse, it looks like the page has a bug: the first reading was that the site had somehow started an edit. The browser's fault is charged to the site, and the reader's concentration is broken either way.

t: A security prompt that asks you to approve a command it does not explain, and cuts off
m: Claude app (iPhone and iPad) · high · open
x: The person is asked to make a security decision and given only code to make it with, partly hidden, on a phone. In practice the choice is to stop the work or to trust blindly, and every prompt like this teaches the habit of pressing Allow without reading, which defeats the point of asking. Here the command was harmless (a one-line edit to two files), but the prompt would have looked the same if it were not.

t: One unlabelled X throws away the whole recording, with no confirmation
m: Claude app (iPhone and iPad) · high · open
x: A minute of dictation, often the hardest part of the message, is gone in one tap, on the button that looks least consequential. It has already happened to the reporter: "I literally fell for this in the past."

t: The live transcript sometimes stops while you are still speaking, and nothing says whether it is still recording
m: Claude app (iPhone and iPad) · high · open
x: The reader has to keep a mental check running while they speak, watching for words to appear, and stops trusting the tool whenever they do not. When it fails the recording cannot be recovered or resubmitted, so the loss is total.

t: Content is hidden until JavaScript runs
x: On a slow phone, or for any reader or agent that does not run the script, the page is blank.

t: Two navigation bars, and a 60-link menu that mixes reading with building
x: The reader has to sort the publication from the workshop themselves, twice.

t: Missing pages show the default GitHub Pages 404
x: A mistyped or old link ends the visit on a page that does not even say which site it is.

t: One topic holds more than half the articles
x: A CISO who picks the obvious topic still faces 35 long reads. The classification does not help anyone choose.

t: Tags are not links, and there are no tag pages
x: The most precise way into the archive looks clickable and goes nowhere.

t: Filters cannot be shared
x: You cannot send a contact "the security articles"; you can only send the whole list and an instruction.

t: Series are invisible
x: Readers land in the middle of a story without knowing there is a beginning.

t: There is no "start here" path
x: A newcomer facing 73 long articles has no way to know which five to read first.

t: Cards do not show reading time or format
x: A reader with three minutes cannot tell a note from a 40-minute analysis before opening it.

t: The best reader feature is buried under metadata and a long italic abstract
x: The short version that would let a reader decide is found only by those who already decided to read.

t: The byline names one human; the AI authorship is in the footer
x: A reader who finds the disclosure late reads it as something hidden, on a publication whose pitch is provenance.

t: There is no page that says why the publication exists
x: Readers cannot judge the argument without knowing who is making it and why.

t: Articles join the reader's list without being asked
x: The list stops meaning "what I chose to keep" and becomes a history the reader did not ask for.

t: "Credit can go below zero" reads as a debt
x: Readers hear "you can owe us money", on a site that has not asked them for any.

t: Three different article counts
x: When a site cannot count itself, the reader doubts every other number on it.

t: Opening a persona link adds it to the browser without asking
x: The reader did not choose to become "a founder" on this site; it was done to them.

t: Persona pages are a list, with no story, opinion or next step
x: A persona link is a promise that the site was made for this reader; a list does not keep it.

t: localStorage throws inside the vault app frame, so reader data is lost on reload
x: A reader's notes disappear on reload, the worst failure a note-taking feature can have.

t: The toolbars come back on any small scroll up, taking screen and moving the page
x: The reader scrolls up a line to re-read a sentence and the whole page jumps, the text moves away from their eyes, and a toolbar they did not ask for takes a ninth of the screen. Each time, attention goes to the chrome instead of the text.

t: Whether the toolbars hide depends on how fast you scroll, not how far
x: The reader cannot ask for the state they want. To read with the toolbars hidden they have to flick, lose their place, find it again carefully, and hope the correction does not undo the result. Every attempt takes attention away from the text, which is the opposite of what hiding the toolbars is for.

t: Three voice controls with no labels: the safe one and the send-as-is one sit side by side
m: Claude app (iPhone and iPad) · medium · open
x: Every first use is a guess, and the guess has consequences: a wrong tap either destroys the recording (UX-060) or sends a message full of transcription errors to an agent that will act on it.

t: The version number is shown three times on the first screen
x: Engineering detail repeated where a reader looks first; it reads as a demo, not a publication.

t: A "For agents /llms.txt" strip sits above the masthead
x: Useful to agents, noise to a person, and it takes the most valuable line on the screen.

t: The editor's note is written for someone who read the last two editions
x: The one personal voice on the front page talks past the newcomer the page most needs to win.

t: Links without extensions in one article
x: They depend on the host resolving extensionless paths; on a strict host or a mirror they break.

t: Each article ends with seven next steps instead of one
x: At the moment the reader is most ready to continue, the page makes them choose among seven.

t: Search only matches titles, teasers and tags
x: About 300,000 words are unsearchable; a reader who remembers a phrase cannot find the piece.

t: Author tooling is shown to every reader
x: A tool for the author, printed on every reader's copy.

t: There is no way to say what was missing
x: Scores say what, not why. Requests that would become the next pitches have no channel.

t: "You pay the price" reads as a warning
x: The feature (your rating sets what the page costs you) is a benefit; the wording makes it a threat.

t: The feed is titled for the old site
x: Subscribers see the wrong publication name in their reader.

t: The study page reports a fixed bug as current
x: A visitor reading the study believes the site is broken in a way it no longer is.

t: A vault app can load images and scripts from a site but cannot fetch its data
x: Builders reasonably expect CORS-open data to be readable and discover otherwise in production; apps must snapshot data instead.

t: Query strings break inside the vault host, so filters must live in the route path
x: The usual way to make a filter linkable is not available; each app has to invent a path encoding.

t: A highlight across paragraphs is cut at the first paragraph
x: The reader loses part of what they chose to keep, without being told.

t: Search results show no snippets
x: A reader cannot see why a result matched, so cannot judge it before opening.

t: Stacked tables on a phone lose their column labels
x: Values without labels on a phone: the reader has to remember what each line means.

t: "Ask the article" has never run against a real on-device model
x: The feature is shown to readers on a path nobody has seen work.

t: The transcript is cleaned up in a second pass without saying when, or what changed
m: Claude app (iPhone and iPad) · low · open
x: The reader can no longer tell their own words from the model's interpretation of them, so they cannot tell what to check. For an instruction to an agent, a quietly changed word can change the task.

t: The £5.00 balance chip has no label
x: An amount of money with no explanation reads as a bill or a trap; the synthetic-user study flagged it.

t: The top-up page said "simulated" while asking for money
x: A payment page that says it is not real is a payment page nobody can trust.

t: Articles were published on two domains, and diverged
x: The same publication was more complete on the wrong site.

t: 51 vault images missing across 10 articles
x: Evidence images are the point of an evidence-first article; broken ones undo the claim.

t: Persona links were designed but not live
x: Every contact got the same front page, made for nobody in particular.

t: The masthead line describes a method, not a subject
x: The one line every visitor reads tells them how the site works instead of what it is about.

t: The edition label is older than the articles under it
x: A front page that looks three days stale on the day it was published tells a reader the site is not kept.

t: File-path pills scrolled the whole page sideways at 390 px
x: Sideways scroll on a phone makes every line harder to read and hides the edge of the content.

t: Re-rendering the whole view on every save lost the reader's place
x: A reader who highlights a sentence is thrown somewhere else in an 8,000-word article.

t: A decision comes with what you need to make it
m: Any prompt that asks the reader to decide (allow, pay, share, delete) first says, in plain words, what will happen, what it touches, whether it can be undone, and why it is being asked. The raw detail is there for checking, not as the explanation.
x: Show the prompt to someone for five seconds. Can they say what will happen if they press each button? If they would need to read code to answer, the prompt has failed.

t: Work is never lost to one tap or a silent failure
m: What the reader has made (a recording, a draft, a note) cannot be destroyed by a single unlabelled tap, and is kept when something fails. Destructive actions ask first or can be undone; failures keep the raw capture and offer a retry.
x: Make something, then press every button that could end the flow. Can any one tap destroy it without asking? Cut the network halfway: is what you made still there?

t: The reader can always tell what the system is doing
m: At every moment the interface shows whether it is listening, working, paused, done or failed. A process that stops shows that it stopped; it never just goes quiet.
x: Start a long operation and watch it. If it stalled now, would anything on screen change? Can you tell "still working" from "failed" without waiting for the end?

t: The first screen is for a stranger
m: On a phone, the first screen says what this is, who it is for, and where to go next. The lead is on it. Chrome, metadata and method come after.
x: Open the page at 390×844 with no history. Count the blocks above the lead. Can someone who has never heard of the site say what it is about?

t: Nothing moves that the reader did not move
m: While the reader is reading, the interface holds still. Toolbars, keyboards, banners and panels appear, move or take focus only on a deliberate gesture made for that purpose, never as a side effect of scrolling or reading.
x: Read a long page on a phone or tablet: scroll down, scroll up a little, pause, carry on. Did anything appear, resize, shift or take focus that you did not ask for? Did the text you were reading stay where it was?

t: The same gesture gives the same result, so it can be learned
m: Every interaction behaves the same way every time, triggered by something the reader controls (where they tap, how far they scroll), never by something they cannot see or repeat (how fast they flicked, what state an animation was in).
x: Do the same thing five times: scroll, flick, tap, at slightly different speeds. Did the interface respond the same way each time? Could you reach the state you wanted on the first try?

t: Label the money, and never surprise with a charge
m: Every number that is money says what it is. The first time anything is charged, the reader is told before or as it happens. Wording about balances never reads as debt or threat.
x: Find every currency figure on the page. Does each have a label? Open a page that charges: did anything say so?

t: A default is not an answer
m: Inputs that ask the reader's opinion start empty. Only what the reader actually did is recorded.
x: Open the form fresh. Is any answer already chosen? Submit without touching it: what was recorded?

t: Ask before keeping
m: Nothing is added to the reader's lists, profile or storage because they opened something. Keeping is a tap the reader makes.
x: Open a page, close it. Did anything appear in the reader's list, board or persona set?

t: Every view is a link
m: Anything a reader can see, they can send: a filter, a search, a tag, a desk, a part of a series. The address changes when the view does.
x: Choose a filter. Copy the address. Open it in a private window. Is it the same view?

t: No dead ends
m: Everything that looks like a way in is one: tags link to pages, missing pages offer the way back, each article ends with one next step.
x: Click every pill, chip and label on a page. Visit a URL that does not exist. Reach the end of an article: what is the one next step?

t: One source of truth for every fact
m: Each piece of content is published once, at one canonical address. Every count, date and label is generated from one manifest at build time.
x: Find the same number on three pages (article count, edition date, version). Do they agree? Does each article have exactly one canonical?

t: The publication is not the workshop
m: Reader pages carry reader things. How the site is built (versions, author tooling, agent strips, release history, admin) lives in one clearly separate area, one link away.
x: List every element on a reader page that only the author or an agent needs. Each one is a finding.

t: Feedback reaches someone, and the reader gets a receipt
m: Every rating, request or 'what is missing' goes somewhere a person reads it, by default and with plain consent, and the reader keeps a receipt of what was sent.
x: Rate something. Where did it go? Who reads it, and when? What does the reader have to show they sent it?

t: Say how long, and what kind, before the reader commits
m: Every card and every link to a long piece shows reading time and format. Every long piece opens with a short version.
x: Look at a list of articles. Can you tell which is a five-minute note and which is a 40-minute analysis?

t: Say who wrote it, and how
m: The byline names the person and the way the piece was made (with agents, from voice notes), where the reader looks, not in the footer. The purpose of the publication is one link away.
x: From the top of any article, can a reader tell who wrote it, with what help, and why the publication exists?

t: Content is visible without waiting for scripts
m: The page renders its content in HTML and shows it at once. Scripts enhance; they never gate what the reader can see.
x: Load the page with JavaScript off, and on a throttled connection. Is the content there at once?

t: What a page says about the present is true now
m: Labels like 'edition of', 'currently', 'broken' and 'live' are dated or generated, and change when the facts do. A fixed problem is marked fixed, with the version.
x: Find every claim about now on the page. Is each dated? Is each still true?

t: A vault app works inside the host, not just on its own
m: An app is tested where readers open it: inside the vault host's sandboxed frame. Routing never assigns location.hash, storage goes through the host, and network reads come from the vault.
x: Open the published vault in the host, click every link, save something, reload. Check the console.

t: Safari on iPad hides its toolbars the same way every time, after a small scroll
Dictation that shows your words as you speak them
Why this exists
m: Who writes ux.sgit.ai, why the register is public, what it is not, and the licences.

t: How it is built
m: How ux.sgit.ai is built and checked: the source files, the build, the gate, and what CI enforces.

t: Versions
m: The release history of ux.sgit.ai: each version, its date, what it changed and the files it touched.

t: Browse
m: Every index of the register in one place: by product, area, problem, visibility, recommendation, principle, severity, status and kind, each value with its count and a link to the filtered list.

t: What good looks like
m: Things that work, each kept as the reference for the findings it answers: measured like a finding, with why it works and what it still does not do.

t: Findings
m: The register: every UX failure and gap found on the sgit.ai sites, with status, severity, the principle it breaks and the fix. Filterable, and every filter is a link.

t: The Newsroom Design Lab
m: Four encrypted vaults that try the newsroom review's fixes as working prototypes, on the real newsroom data, in three design directions each, before anything changes on the live site.

t: Method
m: How a UX finding is made here: the reader's path, the stranger test, the review panel, what severity and status mean, and how to file a finding in the register.

t: Principles
m: The rules the findings break, each with why it matters, a one-minute test you can run on any page, and the findings that break it.

t: Reviews
m: The full UX reviews the findings come from, published whole, with their date, the version reviewed and the method.

t: Newsroom UX review, 11 October 2026
m: The UX review of newsroom.sgit.ai (v0.6.4, re-checked on v0.7.1) that seeded this site's register: first visit, findability, the article and its feedback, personas, reader primitives, the publishing pipeline and a roadmap.
